summary: In situ OAM (IOAM) records telemetry in packets as they cross a network. This document describes how IOAM data fields are carried in IPv6, using IPv6 extension header options.

plainLanguage.summary: As a packet travels, each stop can jot a note on it, such as the time. This says where in an IPv6 packet those notes go.

questions: how does ioam work in ipv6
subtitle: How IPv6 packets carry in-band telemetry notes in hop-by-hop and destination options.

tldr.problem: In situ OAM (IOAM) records telemetry in the packet itself as it crosses a path, but IPv6 needs a defined place and format to carry those IOAM data fields.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9486 puts the IOAM data fields in IPv6 options: Option-Type 0x31 (hop-by-hop) and 0x11 (destination) with an IOAM Opt-Type byte that says which IOAM option follows. It also sets deployment rules for IOAM-Domains.
tldr.outcome: Operators get a standard way to carry IOAM in IPv6 inside a controlled domain, with rules to stop the data leaking out. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 9486 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2023, and it has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: What This RFC Adds to IOAM
sections.content:
In situ Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (IOAM) records operational and telemetry information in the packet while it travels between two points in the network. The concepts and the IOAM Data-Fields themselves are defined in RFC 9197.

RFC 9486 covers one narrow job: how those data fields are encapsulated in IPv6 (RFC 8200), and what a network must do to deploy IPv6-encapsulated IOAM safely. It says IOAM in IPv6 is used to enhance diagnostics and complements other mechanisms such as the IPv6 Performance and Diagnostic Metrics (PDM) Destination Option in RFC 8250.
sections.plainLanguage: The big rulebook already says what notes a packet can carry. This short RFC only says where in an IPv6 packet those notes get pinned.

sections.title: The IOAM Option Format
sections.content:
IOAM data is carried in IPv6 extension headers, either the hop-by-hop options header or the destination options header. Several options with the same option type MAY appear in one such header, as long as their content is distinct. A packet with IOAM can also carry other extension headers that comply with RFC 8200.

The option has an 8-bit Option-Type, an 8-bit Opt Data Len (the option length in octets, not counting the first 2 octets), an 8-bit Reserved field that MUST be zero when sent by the source, an 8-bit IOAM Opt-Type taken from RFC 9197, and then variable-length Option Data specific to the option type.

All of these options must be aligned on multiples of 4 bytes, so the fields from RFC 9197 sit at a multiple-of-4 offset from the start of the options header. Because an IPv6 option can be at most 255 octets long, the total IOAM data in one option is also limited to 255 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: The note area has a label that says what kind of note it is and how long it is. The notes must start on neat boundaries, and the whole pile cannot be longer than 255 bytes.

sections.title: Which IOAM Option Types Map Where
sections.content:
Four IOAM option types are mapped onto IPv6. The Pre-allocated Trace Option (RFC 9197 Section 4.4) and the Proof of Transit (POT) option (Section 4.5) are carried as IPv6 options in the hop-by-hop header, with Option-Type 0x31.

The Edge-to-Edge (E2E) option (RFC 9197 Section 4.6) is carried in the destination options header, with Option-Type 0x11. The Direct Export (DEX) option from RFC 9326 is described as a hop-by-hop option, also written with Option-Type 0x11 in the text. In each case, the IOAM Opt-Type field says which of the four options it is.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four kinds of notes. Some are read by every stop along the way, and one kind is only read at the very end of the trip.

sections.title: Deployment Rules for IOAM-Domains
sections.content:
Four numbered considerations (C1 to C4) apply. C1: IOAM MUST be deployed in an IOAM-Domain, a set of nodes that use IOAM, bounded by its edge and expected to be managed by one administrative entity. C2: adding IOAM data MUST NOT change how routers forward packets, including under Equal-Cost Multipath (ECMP). IOAM MUST be explicitly enabled per interface on every node in the domain, and a router MUST ignore IOAM options on an interface that is not enabled.

C3: the MTU of transit routers and switches must be set so that adding IOAM data never triggers an ICMP Packet Too Big message and a dropped packet, and IOAM must not grow packets beyond the path MTU tolerance. C4: RFC 8200 precludes inserting IOAM data into the original IPv6 header of in-flight packets, so a transit node that adds IOAM MUST add an additional IPv6 header and put the IOAM data there.
sections.plainLanguage: Telemetry stickers may only be used inside your own club. Adding them must not send the packet down a different road, and the packet must not become too big to fit through the doors.

sections.title: Domains Bounded by Hosts or by Routers
sections.content:
Where the IOAM-Domain edge is at the hosts, the hosts themselves add and remove the IOAM data fields, placing them directly in the IPv6 packet as hop-by-hop or destination options.

Where the edge is at network devices such as routers, those devices add and remove the data. They encapsulate the IOAM Data-Fields in an additional, outer IPv6 header, which fits the C4 rule above.
sections.plainLanguage: Either the sender and receiver themselves put on and take off the stickers, or the post offices at the edge wrap the letter in an extra envelope and put the stickers on that.

sections.title: Security and Trust
sections.content:
The RFC assumes a trust model: any node that adds, removes or modifies IOAM data is assumed to be allowed to. By default, packets with IOAM extension headers MUST NOT leak across the domain boundary, and boundary routers MUST filter both incoming and outgoing traffic that carries IPv6 extension headers with IOAM information. A node should only change IOAM headers on a validated directive from a trusted source.

The security considerations of RFC 9197, RFC 8200, RFC 8250 and RFC 9098 also apply. The IOAM-Domain does not rely on the IP Authentication Header (RFC 4302) to protect IOAM options, and using IOAM with AH is not defined here; future documents may define it.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone inside the club is trusted to write on the stickers, so guards at the door must stop sticker-covered packets from going out or coming in.

sections.title: IANA Option-Type Assignments
sections.content:
IANA assigned two IPv6 Option-Types in the "Destination Options and Hop-by-Hop Options" subregistry. Both are described as "IOAM Destination Option and IOAM Hop-by-Hop Option".

Value 0x11 has act bits 00, chg bit 0 and rest 10001. Value 0x31 has act bits 00, chg bit 1 and rest 10001.
sections.plainLanguage: The official numbering office handed out two ID numbers so that routers can recognise IOAM notes.
